video_title: Imran Khan Isn't Worried About Nvidia's "Circular" Deals
gist: Pro Am Asset Management CIO Imran Khan argues Nvidia's roughly 15x forward multiple already fully discounts its 'circular' ecosystem investments -- zero out a quarter of earnings and it still trades under 20x versus a 25-30x history -- while the real bubble sits in new capital issuance, private marks and M&A prices. He frames memory as a story that has gone from a 10 to an 8 (margin expansion done, buyback questions dominating) and Salesforce as a 1 going to 3 with accelerating growth at a 20% discount to Microsoft, and warns that off-balance-sheet private credit has spread AI risk from five megacaps to Goldman Sachs, Blackstone and KKR. Host Dan Nathan is the more bearish voice, calling himself a bear on the allocation of resources rather than on the technology.

insights.claim: Nvidia guided to roughly 70% year-over-year revenue growth for next year versus street consensus near 45%, after beating the quarter by more than $4 billion, and said demand runs above even that guide.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: An unusually early next-year guide 25 points above consensus is the strongest available answer to the durability question that gates every AI trade; watch whether sell-side FY27 revenue converges to the 70% number.

insights.claim: Nvidia trading near 15x a roughly $15 GAAP EPS estimate for fiscal 2028 (calendar 2027) means the market is already discounting its circular ecosystem revenue rather than ignoring it.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: If the circular-deal critique is already in the price, incremental circular-deal headlines are not a new short catalyst; the asymmetry sits with buyers if the deals prove additive.
insights.quote: I think it's already priced in.

insights.claim: Assigning zero value to the roughly 25% of Nvidia revenue tied to companies it invests in still leaves about $12-and-change of EPS and a sub-20x multiple, versus Nvidia's 25-30x historical range, implying roughly $300 on the historical multiple.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete downside-stress valuation floor: haircut a quarter of the business entirely and the stock is still cheap against its own history.

insights.claim: Nvidia is now roughly 14% of the S&P 500, and institutional diversification limits mean funds structurally cannot size up further, capping the multiple regardless of fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Index concentration is itself a valuation headwind; expect flows into second-derivative AI names rather than more Nvidia from large-cap managers.

insights.claim: Nvidia's investment dollars do two distinct jobs: diversify its customer base away from the five hyperscalers and lock up supply chain capacity so competitors cannot build competing silicon at scale.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Reframes 'circular financing' as customer diversification plus supply-chain exclusion -- a moat metric to monitor via non-hyperscaler revenue mix.

insights.claim: OpenAI can design a competitive inference chip but cannot obtain the memory and components to build it at scale, because Nvidia is TSMC's largest customer and has locked up supply chain capacity.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Custom-silicon headlines are a weak bear case for Nvidia until a challenger demonstrates secured memory and foundry capacity; watch supply agreements, not benchmark claims.
insights.quote: OpenAI will not be able to build jalapeno because they don't have access to supply chain.

insights.claim: Buying Nvidia is buying the entire AI ecosystem rather than a GPU manufacturer, and if Nvidia fails it is hard to see how AI works at all.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Positions Nvidia as the index expression of AI rather than a component supplier -- which argues against pair-trading it short against other AI names.
insights.quote: So when you're buying Nvidia, you are not buying GPU maker. You are buying AI ecosystem.

insights.claim: The circular structure runs through four nodes: Nvidia's largest customer OpenAI is also a company Nvidia invests in; Microsoft is OpenAI's largest investor and OpenAI is Microsoft's largest Azure AI customer; and Nvidia is CoreWeave's largest investor, sole GPU supplier, backstop of its sales and buyer of its excess unused compute, while CoreWeave's largest customer is Microsoft.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Maps the two single points of failure -- Nvidia and OpenAI -- so stress-testing the AI complex means stress-testing those two counterparties, not the sector broadly.

insights.claim: The bear case worth holding on AI is about capital allocation, not the technology itself.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Separates the product thesis from the financing thesis -- you can be long AI adoption and short the funding structures built around it.
insights.quote: I'm not a bear on the technology, I'm a bear on the allocation of resources.

insights.claim: The useful economic life of deployed GPUs is probably longer than consensus assumes because the industry is supply-constrained -- a better chip cannot be manufactured at scale quickly -- and investors are focused on demand while ignoring supply.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Longer residual life directly supports GPU-collateralized lending and depreciation schedules; a supply loosening would be the first sign that underwriting is wrong.
insights.quote: the world is compute shortage. Like there's an incredible shortage in compute.

insights.claim: If GPUs are genuinely fungible across customers, the AI-factory model plus revenue-share agreements taking 10-15% of customer revenue would materially change Nvidia's business economics toward high-margin recurring revenue.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A shift from unit sales to revenue share would justify a structurally higher multiple; watch for the first disclosed revenue-share contract.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are deliberately keeping AI build-out debt off their balance sheets, which is what is driving the private credit boom, with KKR, Apollo, BlackRock and Goldman's David Solomon convened by Jensen and willing to backstop chip purchases.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The marginal buyer of AI capex risk is private credit, not equity holders -- so credit spreads on these structures are the better early-warning indicator than tech equity prices.

insights.claim: The direction of a story matters more than its quality: a company rated 10 out of 10 whose story slips to an 8 tends to underperform, while a company rated 1 whose story improves to a 3 can be a phenomenal stock.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for rotation: buy improving narratives at low bases, avoid deteriorating narratives at high bases regardless of business quality.
insights.quote: if a company is like 10 for 10, when the story goes from 10 to 8, those stocks tend to underperform.

insights.claim: Memory's margin-expansion phase is over -- gross margins are near a level unlikely to rise much further -- so future upside has to come from revenue and multiple expansion rather than the demand-plus-margin combination that drove the last year.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Owning memory here means underwriting a re-rating, which the speaker calls a hard way to make money; reduce or rotate rather than chase.
insights.quote: Like buying a stock based on multiple expansion is a tough way of making money.

insights.claim: In group meetings with 30-35 investors in South Korea, roughly 70% of the questions were about share buybacks and 30% about long-term agreements, signalling that the buy side has already concluded the memory margin story has played out.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Question mix at group meetings is a free sentiment indicator; buyback-dominated Q&A marks the late stage of a fundamental cycle.
insights.quote: every question was about share buyback. That's probably 70% of the questions.

insights.claim: Micron went from negative gross margins to roughly 85% gross margins, an extraordinary pricing-power swing for a deeply cyclical business, alongside a roughly 1,000% move in the stock.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan and Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Anchors how much of the memory move was margin-driven and therefore not repeatable -- the base effect makes further upside dependent on volume, not price.
insights.quote: Went from negative to 85% gross margin.

insights.claim: Salesforce's headline numbers were unremarkable but its growth rate accelerated by a point to the 12-14% range with seat count, margins and stock-based compensation discipline all improving -- a one-going-to-three story rather than a confirmed inflection.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Direction of travel, not absolute growth, is what re-rates a de-rated SaaS name; track the acceleration continuing for another quarter before calling the inflection.

insights.claim: On roughly $10 of guided EPS this year and about $12 next year at 20% growth, Salesforce near $240 trades at roughly 20x GAAP earnings -- a 20% discount to Microsoft -- after falling from a $360 all-time high in mid-2024 to $150 months ago.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan and Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Frames the entry multiple explicitly on GAAP rather than non-GAAP earnings, and sets Microsoft as the relative-value benchmark for the SaaS re-rating trade.

insights.claim: Software companies now face a second toll layer: having already accepted paying cloud providers in the on-premise-to-cloud shift, they must now pay the AI labs, so the investable question is whether they can raise prices or cut costs enough to offset it.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A margin screen for all of SaaS -- separate the vendors with pricing power to pass the token bill through from those absorbing it via headcount cuts.
insights.quote: Now we are have to pay a toll to Dario, right?

themes.theme: Where the bubble is and where the ROI is

insights.claim: The bubble sits in new capital issuance, private-market valuations and M&A acquisition prices -- with Celsius valued near $40 billion and Corsair acquired for $60 billion cited as examples -- not in the valuations of the largest and most durable businesses.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Locates the froth in primary issuance and private marks, arguing public megacap longs and private/late-stage exposure require completely different risk treatment.
insights.quote: it's hard to argue that the company who's building the AI ecosystem, Nvidia is trading at a 15 times, that's bubble.

insights.claim: New-issue capital was about 1% of total market capitalization in 1999, and the current volume of debt and equity being raised by AI-linked companies is approaching that same level.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A quantifiable froth gauge that does not depend on multiples -- track issuance as a share of market cap rather than P/E to time the cycle.
insights.quote: in 1999, 1% of the capital market was new issue capital

insights.claim: Because Goldman Sachs, Blackstone and KKR are now funding AI build-outs, the risk has been spread far beyond the five megacaps, so a failure becomes a broad macro event rather than a contained tech drawdown.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Hedging AI risk via short tech equity understates the exposure; the transmission channel is private credit and the banks lending into it.
insights.quote: it's not only meta going to hold the bag. Everybody going to hold the bag

insights.claim: Neo clouds and Oracle would be the first casualties in a demand pullback, and the combination of dot-com-style enthusiasm with financial-crisis-style structuring makes the eventual unwind worse than 2000.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Identifies the weakest links to avoid or short, and argues the financialization layer -- not the technology cycle -- is what makes this drawdown different.
insights.quote: Some of these core like some of these neo clouds are going to be dead. They're going to be the first casualties.

insights.claim: Advertising is the clearest near-term proof of AI ROI because roughly 99% of ad impressions are wasted, so even a 50 basis point improvement in effectiveness drives large revenue gains and lets platforms cut ad load, boosting usage.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Ad platforms are where AI capex converts to measurable P&L first -- a concrete place to underwrite ROI rather than waiting on enterprise agent adoption.
insights.quote: 99% of the ad people see is wasted

insights.claim: Deep domain expertise does not make someone a good stock picker and creates massive blind spots, which is why several of the greatest investors the speaker has met are not experts in any single industry.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A warning for sector specialists: over-knowledge of a company tends to produce overthinking about second-order details rather than the fundamental direction that moves the stock.
insights.quote: being a domain expertise doesn't make you a good stock picker.

insights.claim: Focusing on reported numbers rather than narrative is what has worked over seven and a half years of running the fund, because narrative-driven buying and selling causes investors to miss incremental fundamental change.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Applied to this market: the circular-deal narrative on Nvidia and the SaaS-apocalypse narrative on Salesforce both diverge from the reported numbers.
insights.quote: Let the numbers guide you as opposed to narrative guide you.

insights.claim: Buying a stock purely because it is cheap has been the speaker's single biggest mistake; valuation should be read as a reflection of consensus rather than as a reason to buy, with entry justified by improving fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: Reframes multiples as sentiment data -- Nvidia at 15x reads as the market pricing circular risk, and Salesforce at 15x on $10 read as the market pricing a going-concern problem.

insights.claim: If a story cannot be explained to an investor in 60 seconds or less, it is not a good stock -- a filter that disqualifies positions requiring complex structural arguments.
insights.speaker: Imran Khan
insights.so_what: A practical complexity filter: theses needing elaborate explanation usually depend on multiple expansion, which is the hard way to make money.
insights.quote: If I can't explain a story to an investors in 60 seconds or less, it's not a good stock.
